newsitem.title: USA: DC mayor defends restructuring of city bond debt.
newsitem.headline: DC mayor defends restructuring of city bond debt.

text.p: District of Columbia Mayor Marion Barry on Monday defended his proposal to restructure outstanding city debt in order to balance D.C.'s budget in fiscal 1998 as sound, but a Moody's bond rating agency official called the move "risky."

"This is not a budget gimmick," Barry said at a press briefing on the $3.3 billion FY 1998 budget he sent this weekend to the city's congressionally mandated financial control board for review. He said, New York and Philadelphia refinanced "major amounts of debt" during the first two years that they were under control panels.

But Barbara Flickinger, a vice president at Moody's Investors Service in charge of D.C. ratings, warned that stretching out the city's debt repayment schedule could "saddle" D.C. with longer payments and higher interest rates.

"Generally we view debt restruturing negatively," said Flickinger, one of several Wall Street rating agencies that have given the city's debt a "junk" rating. "It limits flexibility down the road" particularly if the new funds are being used as a bandaid for immediate problems.

But Barry said it would be "devastating" to public safety, education and other key services if the city does not not find an additional $50 million in FY 98 through restructuring of about $300 million in debt.
"Do they want blood in the streets? Do they want people dying in their homes?" Barry asked at the press briefing.
Barry's plan already has run into hot water with the city's congressionally appointed chief financial officer, Anthony Williams.

In a letter accompanying the proposed budget, Williams warned Barry that restructuring city debt without resolving massive problems like the city's unfunded pension liability first will be "poorly received" by Wall Street.
Barry's proposal now goes to the city's five-member control board, which hopes to send a final budget propsal to Congress by the end of March.
